description: We’re from Jakarta building SightLine, a Marswalk planning map for Jezero Crater. We layer real NASA data (HiRISE imagery, CTX terrain, Perseverance traverse and photos, JPL Horizons signal delay, DONKI space weather) into a web map with route tracking, slope and oxygen alerts, and a 3D walk mode. Roles: map & UI, tracking, data & science, 3D/VR. Team complete.
summary:
In 1971, Apollo 14’s crew walked toward Cone Crater, came within about 20 metres of the rim and turned back: every ridge looked like the last one. On Mars it is harder. There is no GPS, and dust hides the hills astronauts steer by.

Sightline is a navigation and safety map for walking in Jezero Crater without GPS. It does three things we have not found together anywhere else:

It shows where you lose sight of home. Red zones, computed from NASA’s Jezero elevation model, mark ground where no landmark is visible, and they grow live as dust rises.
It fixes your position from the hills. With no GPS the suit’s step-count position drifts. Horizon Match compares the outline of the hills the astronaut sees with outlines computed from NASA terrain and shrinks that drift back.
It knows the astronaut’s body. Balance and vision changes after landing, suit time and cooling limits, and solar-storm radiation (NASA measurements) set when to turn back.

Crews will drive rovers too, but rovers break and get stuck. Apollo had a rule for that: never drive further than you can walk back on your suit’s supplies. Sightline is that walk back, on Mars, without GPS.

Today it is a planning tool for walks at Jezero. Next, the same answer belongs inside the helmet, and the same sight-line maps can choose where to put the habitat and radio beacons so no route has blind spots.
details:
• What it does: a map of where you lose sight of home, position fixes from the hills (Horizon Match), a crew model that knows the astronaut’s body, a helmet view, and a walk planner. The planner takes several stops with a stay at each and walk or rover. It shows the day on a dial, finds the best leave time, and lets you move a storm on the dial to see when the crew must turn back.
  • How it works: precomputed viewsheds and skylines from the CTX elevation model (Python/NumPy, with Mars curvature). A live in-browser horizon match on a 40 m grid. An A* route planner with slope limits checked on 40 m terrain and blind-zone penalties. A pure-function crew model where every constant is tagged NASA data or estimate. A Leaflet map on NASA Mars Trek tiles with HiRISE close-ups, and A-Frame/three.js 3D terrain and helmet view.
  • Benefits: a navigation aid that works with no GPS and no comms. It makes “can I get home?” visible, and it is a planning tool for EVA designers.
  • What we hope to achieve: test Horizon Match on real Perseverance Navcam photos; place beacons to remove blind zones; feed live MEDA/DONKI data; AR in suit helmets.
  • Honest limits: Horizon Match was tested on 5 real Perseverance panoramas (3 of them used while developing): 4 were within 51–143 m and one was 2.8 km off. Five is too few to quote an error rate. Several crew-model constants are team estimates, and the app marks each one.
  • Tools: HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Leaflet, A-Frame/three.js, Python, NumPy, Pillow, GitHub Pages, Claude, GitHub Copilot.
